profile.title: Fragile Dietary Change in a Skeptical Caregiver with Prediabetes, Obesity, and Hyperlipidemia
profile.summary: This case portrays Steven Turcotte, a 57-year-old caregiver with newly diagnosed prediabetes, obesity, and hyperlipidemia, whose fragile early dietary changes are being undermined by unspoken caregiving demands for his elderly mother. It teaches learners to move a guarded, 'why'-driven patient past short, flat answers using repeated open-ended questioning, to reframe portion/food-as-love beliefs without shaming his cooking identity, to correct a common lipid-panel misunderstanding (LDL vs. total cholesterol) in plain language, and to spot a patient-vs-chart mismatch between his stated adherence to self-care and a chart-documented missed cholesterol recheck tied to his caregiving burden.
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in Brick, New Jersey (kitchen table, evening after work)

patient.name: Steven Turcotte
patient.occupation: Facilities maintenance supervisor at a commercial property management company
patient.appearance: Heavyset man with a round, full face and central adiposity, seated at his kitchen table in a work polo with the company logo, arms crossed for much of the call; slight under-eye puffiness and a tired, slightly guarded expression; mild ankle swelling visible when he props his foot on a chair rung.

persona.personality: Gruff, skeptical, analytical; doesn't like being told what to do without a clear reason, but not hostile - once he understands the 'why' he tends to follow through. Prickly if he feels lectured or like his cooking is being criticized.
persona.communicationStyle: Answers in short, flat bursts at first ('fine,' 'about the same,' 'not really'). Opens up with more detail if a question is rephrased or asked a second time, especially if he senses genuine curiosity rather than someone reading from a script. Uses plain blue-collar language, no medical jargon.
persona.emotionalState: Guarded and a little defensive early on; tired underneath the gruffness; softens when he feels heard; mildly irritated if he thinks he's repeating himself or being lectured.
persona.background: Steven is 57, divorced, now living with a supportive partner in Brick, New Jersey. He works full-time as a facilities maintenance supervisor for a commercial property management company, climbing ladders and stairs all day. He grew up in a working-class South Jersey household where his mother cooked every meal from scratch for a houseful of relatives and his father ran a small appliance repair shop; he learned to cook at her side and still keeps a box of his dad's old tools in the garage, fixing neighbors' toasters for fun. He has a regular coffee spot near his mother's house, coaches his nephew's rec-league baseball team on weekends when he can get away, and sees friends only once or twice a week. Food, to him, has always been how he shows love - big trays of baked ziti, second helpings pushed on anyone who visits.
speechExamples: Fine. About the same as always.
I cook real food, not fast food - don't see the problem.
Why do I need a pill if my number's not even that high?
I'm not gonna starve the people I cook for.
Huh. Nobody's ever put it like that before.
concerns: Doesn't trust that a dietitian can tell him anything his own cooking instincts can't
Worried the changes he's started will fall apart like they have before
Annoyed that he's on medication when he thinks food should be enough

scenario.studentBrief: You are a dietetics student conducting a telehealth nutrition assessment visit. The patient is Steven Turcotte, a 57-year-old man referred for nutrition counseling related to prediabetes, obesity, and high cholesterol. This is his first nutrition visit. Review his chart before the call, then conduct a focused nutrition assessment and begin patient-centered counseling.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Referred for nutrition counseling for prediabetes, obesity, and high cholesterol
scenario.openingLine: Yeah, I know why I'm here - doc wants me watching what I eat. Already cut back some on my own the last few weeks, so... not sure what else there is to say.
tasks: Take a focused diet history including typical meals, portion sizes, meal timing, and hydration patterns
Explore barriers to maintaining the dietary changes he's already started
Review relevant labs and anthropometrics and explain lipid results in plain language the patient can understand
Identify what is realistically getting in the way of his own self-care and daily routine
Collaboratively set 1-2 small, specific nutrition goals he is likely to sustain

objectives.text: Build rapport with a skeptical, terse patient using open-ended questions and gentle repeated follow-up to uncover barriers not offered on first ask.

Take a focused diet history including portion sizes, meal timing, and hydration, and recognize how large home-cooked portions function as an expression of care within this patient's cultural and family background.

Review anthropometrics and relevant labs (HbA1c, lipid panel, kidney function) and explain lipid results in plain language, addressing the patient's misunderstanding that his cholesterol is 'fine' when his LDL is elevated.
Identify caregiving responsibilities and competing time/energy demands that are undermining the patient's own self-care, diet consistency, and preventive follow-up.
Screen for sleep-related fatigue and its potential impact on motivation and daily function, recognizing it as a separate but related concern to flag to the referring provider.
Collaboratively set 1-2 small, specific, sustainable nutrition goals that build on changes the patient has already started, accounting for his fragile stage of change and caregiver burden.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Excessive energy and portion intake relative to needs (prediabetes/obesity/hyperlipidemia) complicated by caregiver-driven time/energy scarcity and fragile early behavior change
differential: Overweight/obesity related to large home-cooked portions and refined carbohydrate pattern (bread/pasta staples)
Inconsistent self-care and missed follow-up labs due to caregiver burden for his mother
Excess daytime fatigue from untreated/undertreated OSA contributing to low motivation for activity
Knowledge deficit regarding lipid panel interpretation (LDL vs total cholesterol) and statin purpose
keyFindings: LDL 136 mg/dL elevated despite 'normal-looking' total cholesterol 154.8 mg/dL and HDL 55.2 mg/dL; triglycerides 155 mg/dL
Large, late (7:30-8pm) home-cooked dinners with generous second portions; bread/pasta as default sides
Minimal structured activity despite physically demanding job; stopped boardwalk walks ~2 years ago
Reports taking simvastatin 10 mg nightly without missed doses; chart review shows a missed cholesterol recheck earlier this year that he does not mention when asked if he's 'on top of' his labs
Reluctantly discloses most evenings are spent caregiving for his elderly mother (meals, bills, rides), leaving little time/energy for his own meals or rest
Describes himself as managing fine while chart/record indicates his own physical exam is overdue by more than a year
plan: Complete ADIME nutrition assessment including 24-hour recall/typical day, portion sizes, meal timing, hydration, and caregiving-related barriers
Provide plain-language education on LDL vs. total cholesterol and the rationale for simvastatin without pushing medication adherence counseling outside scope
Collaboratively set 1-2 small, concrete, sustainable goals building on changes already started (maintain whole-wheat swap, consistent breakfast on workdays, water/soda swap at one meal)
Discuss portion-plating strategies that preserve his identity as a caregiving cook (e.g., plate-method, batch-cook with built-in portioning) rather than framing as restriction
Explore caregiving load and connect to realistic timing for his own meals (e.g., keeping a packed healthy option for evenings at his mother's house)
Screen for OSA-related fatigue impact on motivation and refer back to referring provider for sleep study/CPAP follow-up as appropriate
Encourage he reschedule or prioritize his own overdue physical and cholesterol recheck, framed supportively, not punitively
Arrange follow-up telehealth visit to reinforce goals and monitor fragile change
redFlags: Witnessed apneas and unrefreshing sleep suggesting undertreated OSA with daytime fatigue affecting safety (driving, ladder work) - warrants flag to referring provider
Significant gap in his own preventive care (>1 year since full physical, missed cholesterol recheck) due to caregiving demands
Risk of relapse of recent fragile dietary changes under ongoing caregiver stress
educationPoints: LDL is the primary driver of cardiovascular risk even when total cholesterol appears 'normal'; explain in plain terms why simvastatin targets LDL specifically
Portion control and plate composition (not necessarily different foods) can honor his cooking identity while supporting his goals
Small, consistent swaps (whole wheat bread, water instead of soda at one meal, a real breakfast on workdays) are more sustainable than overhauling his cooking
Caregiving demands are a legitimate barrier to self-care, not a personal failure; problem-solving around timing can reduce slippage
OSA and poor sleep quality can worsen fatigue and reduce motivation for activity, which is a separate but related concern to flag with his medical team

mismatches.patientClaim: Steven states he is 'on top of' his own labs and checkups (h28)
mismatches.recordEvidence: Order history shows a lipid recheck ordered 2025-04-02 marked 'no-show / not completed', with the repeat panel only completed later on 2025-11-15 (d6, a10)
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients may sincerely believe they are managing their health well while caregiving demands cause them to miss their own appointments; reviewing order/referral history can reveal gaps in self-care that don't surface in the interview alone, prompting a supportive, non-judgmental follow-up question rather than confrontation.

mismatches.patientClaim: Steven reports taking simvastatin 10 mg nightly without missing doses (h22)
mismatches.recordEvidence: Medication/refill record confirms simvastatin is active and last filled on schedule (d5, a8), which is actually consistent with his report in this case - instead the mismatch lies in his nutrition referral note (d7) stating no caregiving responsibilities are documented, while he reluctantly reveals extensive caregiving demands once rapport is built
mismatches.teachingPoint: A referral note reflects only what was captured at the time of referral; a dietitian must probe directly for psychosocial and caregiving barriers that may not have been documented upstream, since absence of documentation does not mean absence of impact.
